title: Little words that carry the tone
goal: Use enclitic particles — one-syllable words that separate a foreigner speaking Tagalog from someone who really speaks it.
bekal: stacking several particles in the right order

notes: **Na and pa are opposites.** *Na* means a change has happened ("already", "now"), *pa* means the old state continues ("still", "not yet"). *Kumain na ako* (I've eaten) versus *Kumakain pa ako* (I'm still eating). These two tiny words do much of the work other languages give to tenses.
**Wala pa means "none yet", wala na means "all gone".** A world of difference. At a shop, *wala na* means you're too late; *wala pa* means it's on its way.

**Naman is the hardest particle to translate and one of the most used.** It softens, contrasts, mildly complains and affirms — depending on tone. *Ang tagal naman* (what's taking so long), *Oo naman* (of course), *Ikaw naman* (your turn; or: oh, you!).

**Lang means "just, only"** and almost always makes things smaller: *sandali lang* (just a moment), *isa lang* (just one), *joke lang* (just kidding). The formal form is *lamang*, used only in formal writing.
**Na lang means "…instead, then"** — the fallback choice after the first plan fails. *Sa 7-Eleven na lang.* This pair is very typical and very common; learn it as one unit.
**Pala marks a discovery.** "Oh, so…", "turns out". *May sunblock pala ako* = turns out I have some. It's always about information you've just realized, never about something you already knew.

**Daw / raw means "they say, apparently"** and passes responsibility for the information to someone else. *Sarado raw* = apparently it's closed — not my claim. In a culture that avoids confrontation, like the Philippines, this particle works hard.
**Eh at the end of a sentence gives a reason** and asks for understanding, a bit like "you know" or "though": *Male-late na tayo, eh.* It never starts a sentence.

**Nga emphasizes and urges.** *Tara na nga!* (come on, hurry!), *Oo nga* (yes, that's right), *Pakiulit nga* (could you repeat that). The tone can be warm or impatient — your ear decides, not the dictionary.

grammars.title: The most common particles
body: They all attach after the first word of the sentence and never stand alone at the front.
after: *Sana* deserves attention: it expresses hope (*sana maganda ang panahon* — hopefully the weather's nice) as well as regret (*sana pumunta ka kahapon* — if only you'd come yesterday). Context tells them apart.
*Yata* is the softest way to say something you're not sure of. Its cousins are *siguro* (maybe) and *parang* (it seems, kind of).
All these particles can be stacked freely — and native speakers do stack them.

grammars.title: Order when there's more than one particle
body: There is a fixed order, and breaking it makes your sentence sound scrambled. The basic rule: **one-syllable words first, two-syllable words after.**
after: You only need three often: *ka na ba*, *na po* and *na lang*. Master these and ninety percent of your everyday sentences will already sound natural.
⚠️ If the first word takes a linker, the particle goes **before** the linker: *Wala na**ng** tinapay* (there's no more bread), not *walang na tinapay*.
Placing particles correctly is one of the quickest signs that someone really speaks Tagalog rather than translating from English in their head.

sections.title: Na and pa in everyday sentences

blocks.text: Look at the last row: *tama na* (that's enough) and *konti pa* (a little more) are the two sentences you'll say most at a Filipino dinner table — the first to stop your host, the second to ask them to keep going.
*Naman* deserves its own page, because it's the one particle with no fixed English equivalent at all.

blocks.title: Why these particles matter
items: Tagalog conveys politeness and warmth through particles, not through word choice as Japanese or Javanese do, or through sentence form as English does ("could you possibly…").

A grammatically perfect sentence with no particles sounds cold, stiff and slightly scary — like an airport announcement. Adding *naman*, *po* or *lang* instantly turns it into a conversation between people.
This is the part of the language no table can teach, this one included. You learn it by listening to people talk — teleseryes, vlogs and chats at the corner shop.
